newsitem.title: GERMANY: Buba's Koebnick says no reserve cut should be made.
newsitem.headline: Buba's Koebnick says no reserve cut should be made.

text.p: The Bundesbank should not cut its minimum reserve requirement soon since a reduction may scuttle efforts to have the future European central bank use reserves too, a Bundesbank official said.

"The founding fathers of Europe's planned currency union have intended that there should be a minimum reserve requirement, and the Bundesbank has already taken a set of steps to ready its own reserve requirements for Europe," Bundesbank council member Hans-Juergen Koebnick told Reuters in an interview on Wednesday.

Koebnick argued that it would be counterproductive to scale back Germany's own reserve requirements at a time Bundesbank and government officials are insisting that the future European central bank must use a similar type of requirement.

"It would be legitimate to ask whether one would not run the risk of completely sabotaging the concept of minimum reserves if Germany were to cut its own requirement again," Koebnick, also the president of the state central bank in the Rhineland and Saar regions, said.

The Bundesbank requires banks to hold minimum reserves on short-term borrowings obtained from foreign banks or domestic non-banks in non-interest bearing accounts at the central bank generally prompting banks to conduct such operations abroad.
Currently the reserve level is two percent on sight and term deposits and 1.5 percent on savings deposits, having been pared back several times.

German commercial banks, complaining that the Bundesbank's reserve requirements put them at a competitive disadvantage, have repeatedly called for another reduction in the reserve requirement or even doing away with it altogether.
But Koebnick said even another reduction in minimum reserve requirements would not bring back the business that has already been moved abroad to centres including London.

Instead he suggested that Germany should capitalise on its strengths, including a competent banking supervisory commission which prohibits "the lapses that have occurred in other nations", to improve its image as a financial centre.

Similarly Koebnick also said that no more changes were planned for recently introduced short-term government debt, another innovation which banks said was necessary to transform Germany into a more competitive financial centre.
The six-month Treasury discount paper, first auctioned in June, is not listed on the bourse and was initially limited in volume to 20 billion marks a year.
"We do not want to get into a situation of short-termism," Koebnick said, referring to the practice of financing largely with short-term paper.
The Bundesbank had long opposed the issue of short term debt as it feared this could undermine its monetary policy.

But Koebnick said the paper's volume could be increased as the Bundesbank council had agreed that state governments will also be allowed to issue up to a total of 20 billion marks in short-term debt per year.
This would raise the total volume of annually issued short-term debt to 40 billion marks, Koebnick said.
Koebnick however did not say whether plans are underway to possibly list the paper on the bourse and make it more attractive for banks.
